people/john-livingstone-nevius/summary: Missionary in Shandong whose Methods of Mission Work (1886) urged self-supporting, self-propagating churches led by unpaid local leaders. Adopted by Presbyterian missionaries in Korea after his visit in 1890, the "Nevius plan" is credited with shaping the strongly indigenous Korean Protestant church.
people/john-livingstone-nevius/keyIdeas/: Bible study system for lay leaders
people/roberto-de-nobili/summary: Italian Jesuit in Madurai who adopted the dress, diet and lifestyle of a Brahmin sannyasi, learned Tamil and Sanskrit, and allowed converts to keep caste customs he judged social rather than religious. His method, contested by fellow missionaries, was approved by Gregory XV (1623) and later restricted in the Malabar Rites controversy (1704–1744).
people/roberto-de-nobili/keyIdeas/1: Distinction between civil and religious customs
people/hendrik-kraemer/roles/2: first director of the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey
people/hendrik-kraemer/summary: Dutch Reformed lay missiologist and scholar of Islam in Java whose The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World (1938), written for the Tambaram conference, argued under Barth’s influence for "biblical realism": the radical discontinuity between the gospel and all religions.
people/lesslie-newbigin/roles/1: bishop in the Church of South India
people/lesslie-newbigin/summary: Scottish missionary who became a bishop of the united Church of South India (1947), helped integrate the International Missionary Council into the WCC (1961), and in retirement in Birmingham argued that the West itself had become a mission field. The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989) defended Christian particularity against pluralism and called the congregation "the hermeneutic of the gospel".
people/lesslie-newbigin/keyIdeas/0: Missio Dei and mission to the West
people/lesslie-newbigin/keyIdeas/2: Congregation as hermeneutic of the gospel
people/lamin-sanneh/summary: Gambian-born scholar, a convert from Islam, whose Translating the Message (1989) argued that Christianity’s commitment to vernacular Bible translation made it a force for indigenous cultural renewal rather than simply a tool of colonialism. Whose Religion Is Christianity? (2003) described the emergence of world Christianity.
people/rene-padilla/roles/1: leader of the Latin American Theological Fraternity
people/rene-padilla/summary: Ecuadorian-born Argentine Baptist theologian whose address at Lausanne (1974), with Samuel Escobar’s, challenged North American evangelism as culturally captive and called for "integral mission" (misión integral), joining evangelism and social responsibility under the kingdom of God.
people/rene-padilla/keyIdeas/2: Kingdom of God as framework of mission
people/leonard-feeney/roles/1: founder of the Slaves of the Immaculate Heart of Mary
people/leonard-feeney/summary: Boston Jesuit who taught a strict reading of "outside the Church there is no salvation", denying salvation to any who die without explicit membership in the Catholic Church. The Holy Office’s letter to Archbishop Cushing (1949) rejected his interpretation; he was excommunicated for disobedience (1953) and reconciled in 1972.
people/adolf-von-harnack/summary: Baltic German church historian whose History of Dogma (1886–90) argued that dogma was the work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the gospel, and whose lectures What Is Christianity? (1900) distilled liberal Protestantism: the fatherhood of God, the infinite value of the human soul and the commandment of love. His former student Karl Barth broke with him after Harnack signed the 1914 manifesto supporting the German war effort.
people/adolf-von-harnack/keyIdeas/1: The kernel and husk of the gospel
people/adolf-von-harnack/keyIdeas/2: Fatherhood of God and brotherhood of man
people/j-gresham-machen/summary: Princeton New Testament scholar (The Origin of Paul’s Religion, 1921; The Virgin Birth of Christ, 1930) whose Christianity and Liberalism (1923) argued that liberalism was not a version of Christianity but a different religion. After Princeton Seminary was reorganised (1929) he founded Westminster Theological Seminary and, after his suspension from the ministry, the Orthodox Presbyterian Church (1936).
people/j-gresham-machen/keyIdeas/1: Historic Christianity as a redemptive religion grounded in historical facts
people/harry-emerson-fosdick/summary: The most famous liberal Protestant preacher in America. His sermon "Shall the Fundamentalists Win?" (21 May 1922), preached at First Presbyterian Church in New York, pleaded for tolerance of liberal views on the virgin birth, inerrancy and the second coming and ignited the Fundamentalist–Modernist controversy in the Presbyterian Church. He later served as pastor of Riverside Church (1930–46), and wrote the hymn "God of Grace and God of Glory".
people/thomas-campbell/summary: Ulster Seceder Presbyterian minister who emigrated to western Pennsylvania (1807), was censured for offering communion to other Presbyterians, and founded the Christian Association of Washington, whose Declaration and Address (1809) called for Christian unity on the basis of the Bible alone. With his son Alexander he became a founder of the Stone-Campbell Restoration Movement.
people/thomas-campbell/keyIdeas/0: Unity through restoring New Testament Christianity
people/thomas-campbell/keyIdeas/2: Rejection of creeds as tests of fellowship
people/pius-x/summary: Giuseppe Sarto, pope from 1903 to 1914, who condemned Catholic Modernism in the decree Lamentabili and the encyclical Pascendi Dominici Gregis (1907), imposed the Anti-Modernist Oath on clergy (1910), encouraged frequent communion and the admission of children to communion, and began the codification of canon law. He was canonised in 1954.
people/john-r-mott/roles/1: YMCA and Student Volunteer Movement leader
people/john-r-mott/summary: American Methodist layman who led the Student Volunteer Movement and the World Student Christian Federation, popularised the watchword "the evangelization of the world in this generation", chaired the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh (1910) and helped found the International Missionary Council and the World Council of Churches.
people/andrew-walls/summary: Scottish historian who taught in Sierra Leone and Nigeria and founded the Centre for the Study of Christianity in the Non-Western World (Aberdeen, later Edinburgh). His essays argued that Christianity is infinitely translatable, that its history is serial (its centre repeatedly moving), and that the 20th-century shift of its centre to Africa, Asia and Latin America is the most important development in recent church history.
people/rachel-held-evans/summary: American writer raised in evangelical Tennessee whose books and blog (Faith Unraveled, 2010; A Year of Biblical Womanhood, 2012; Searching for Sunday, 2015; Inspired, 2018) gave voice to a generation questioning evangelical certainties about Scripture, gender, science and politics; she joined the Episcopal Church and became an emblematic figure in "deconstruction" and progressive Christianity before her early death.
people/william-paley/summary: English Anglican clergyman whose Natural Theology (1802) made the classic argument from design — the watch found on a heath — and whose Evidences of Christianity (1794) was required reading at Cambridge, where Charles Darwin studied it closely.
people/joseph-butler/summary: English bishop whose Analogy of Religion (1736) answered the deists by arguing that the difficulties found in revealed religion are paralleled in nature, which deists accepted as God’s work; since certainty is unavailable, probability is the guide of life.
people/david-hume/summary: Scottish Enlightenment philosopher raised in the Church of Scotland who became its most formidable sceptical critic: his essay “Of Miracles” (1748) and posthumous Dialogues concerning Natural Religion (1779) attacked the evidential case for miracles and the design argument.
people/soren-kierkegaard/summary: Danish Lutheran writer who attacked both Hegelian rational Christianity and the complacent state church. Through pseudonymous works such as Fear and Trembling (1843) and Concluding Unscientific Postscript (1846) he argued that faith is a passionate, subjective commitment to the “absolute paradox” of the God-man, not the conclusion of objective proof.
people/emil-brunner/summary: Swiss Reformed theologian, early ally of Karl Barth in dialectical theology, whose Nature and Grace (1934) argued for a “point of contact” for the gospel in human nature and a limited natural knowledge of God, provoking Barth’s furious “No!”. He later taught at International Christian University in Tokyo (1953-55).
people/emil-brunner/keyIdeas/1: Formal and material image of God
people/cornelius-van-til/summary: Dutch-born American Reformed apologist at Westminster Theological Seminary who developed presuppositional apologetics: since all reasoning rests on ultimate commitments, Christians should argue transcendentally that only the triune God of Scripture makes logic, science and morality intelligible.
people/alvin-plantinga/summary: American Reformed philosopher (Calvin College, Notre Dame) whose free-will defence (1974) answered the logical problem of evil and whose “Reformed epistemology” (Faith and Rationality, 1983; Warranted Christian Belief, 2000) argues that belief in God can be properly basic and warranted without evidential argument.
